coach_says: Your bishop on f2 is pinned: the rook on f1 is lined up behind it with your king on the f-file. Kf5 keeps the king on that file, so Rf3+ checks you and then White simply takes the pinned bishop with two rooks against your one defender. Step the king off the f-file first (Ke6, Ke5 or Kg6) so the bishop is free to move and the position stays level.

Your d6 pawn was under fire from the e5 pawn, and White's queen on d5 was sitting in front of the rook on d1. Offering the queen trade with Qc6 takes that queen off the d-file: after Qxc6 bxc6 exd6 your bishop is attacked and can't take back on d6, because the rook on d1 now sees straight down the open file. You end up a pawn down against a monster passed pawn on d6, and c5 falls too. Before trading, ask which files and lines the trade opens; Qe8 or b6 kept the d-file blocked.

White's d5 pawn was there for the taking with Qxd5. You can't take with the knight because it is pinned to your queen by the bishop on g5, but the queen can capture, and after Nc3 you swap queens with Qxd1+ and stay two pawns up with an easy game. Bd6 is a fine developing move, but when the opponent leaves a pawn loose in a gambit, check whether you can just take it safely.

You were already a pawn down, and c5 puts another pawn where nothing protects it: the bishop on f8 can take it straight away with Bxc5, developing with tempo at the same time. Before pushing a pawn, check whether the square it lands on is defended. Developing with Bd3 or Nd2 and getting castled was the way to fight for the lost pawn.

White's queen on f5 and bishop on d3 both aim at h7, and the threat was Qh7+ Kf8 Qh8 mate, since your own queen on e7 blocks the king's escape. Bxb2 grabs a pawn but does nothing about it, so you get mated in two. Every move, ask what your opponent is threatening first: g6 blocks the bishop's diagonal, and Kf8 or Qf6 also deal with the mate.

Before recapturing, count who guards your knight on e5. It was attacked by the knight on f3 and the bishop on b2, and defended by your bishop on d6 and your queen on e7. Qxd7 pulls the queen away, so now it is two attackers against one defender and Nxe5 wins a piece. Kxd7 looks odd, but it recaptures while keeping the queen guarding e5, and you are fine.

White's knight on f3 is already attacking your e5 pawn, and Bc5 does nothing to protect it, so Nxe5 just takes a central pawn. You may win it back later with tricks like Qe7 hitting e4, but you spend time doing so while White develops. When a pawn is attacked, defend it first: Nc6 is the natural move, developing and guarding e5 at once.

Your f- and g-pawns are gone, so your king has very little cover and the light squares around it are weak. Bxf3 gives away the bishop that guards those squares and brings White's queen to f3 for free, where it eyes b7 (with your rook on a8 behind it) and h5 with check. Retreating with Bh5 keeps the pin on the knight and keeps your light-squared bishop at home.
also: exposed king on the e8-h5 diagonal

coach_says: Rf4 attacks the bishop on h4, but it just steps to g3 and attacks your rook, so you have spent a move and must spend another getting the rook to safety. Meanwhile White brings a rook to d1 and wins your passed pawn on d3. Your advantage was that d3 pawn: use the time to support it and develop, for example b6 followed by Ba6 to guard d3, and c5 to keep your d4 bishop solid.

Your queen had to move, and it also needed to keep guarding c2 against the Nxc2+ fork of king and rook. Qf2 does guard c2, but Ng4 attacks it again and you are forced into Qd2 while Black develops with tempo. Qd3 guards c2, attacks the d4 knight and has no knight that can easily chase it, so look for a square that does all the jobs and can't be hit right away.

Black's queen on f6 already aims at f2, which only your king defends. After Bb5, Black plays Bc5 and threatens Qxf2 mate, and you have to scramble with Rh2. Bb5 hits a knight that is safely defended and leaves your kingside undeveloped. Nc3 was the move: it threatens Nxe4, winning your pawn back with an attack on the queen, and from e4 the knight also guards f2.

Black's queen went pawn-grabbing on b3 and is short of squares, held in by your knight on c4 and queen on d2. Na5 attacks it, but the knight leaves c4 and the queen just steps to c3, defended by the d4 pawn, and offers a trade, after which Black is simply a pawn up. With a5 you take away b6 and prepare Nb6 hitting the a8 rook, while rooks to b1 or a3 keep squeezing the queen. When the enemy queen is stranded, take squares away from it rather than chasing it out.
concept: keep the stray queen boxed in

coach_says: Nf6 develops a piece and is as good as anything here. The damage was done by Bxf2+, which gave a bishop for a pawn; now just develop quickly, castle and look for chances against White's exposed king.

Bd8 is a reasonable way to save the bishop; it is nearly as good as the engine's choice. The position was already difficult after the queen trade let the d6 pawn in, so here the job is to blockade that pawn and keep your pieces active.
c5 is a perfectly good reply to 1. Nc3, heading for Sicilian-style positions. Nothing to fix here.
Rc1 is the engine's top choice: your back-rank rook was attacked, and this keeps it active while eyeing c7. You were already in a difficult position; this was a good practical move.
g5 is fine and keeps your winning position; it fixes Black's kingside pawns. Bringing the rook to d1 to support your d7 pawn was a touch more precise, but the difference is tiny.
The position was already lost because of White's pawn on f7, and Ne5 is as good a try as any. Nothing a different move here would have saved.

Castling is a natural move, but Black's king is wide open: the f-pawn is gone, so the diagonal from h5 to e8 leads straight to it, and the bishop on f5 has no defender. Nd4 attacks that bishop, and if exd4 then Qh5+ picks it up with check (Nh4 works on the same idea). When the enemy king is exposed and a piece is loose, look for a check that also attacks it before tidying up your own king.
also: exposed king on the e8-h5 diagonal

coach_says: When f6 hit your bishop, retreating with Bf4 lets Black take on e5 and free their position. Taking first is stronger: after exf6 Bxf6 Bxf6 Rxf6, Black's knight on f5 stands in front of the rook on f6, both on the file of your queen on f3. Then g4 attacks the pinned knight, which can't move without losing the rook, and you win material. When a pawn attacks your piece, see whether capturing first creates a pin or a target.
